description: We are a team interesting in making mathematical and AI based solutions.
summary:
Limiar is a web workspace that answers one question for fire-safety engineers: what has NASA actually measured about a flame like this one, and where does the evidence end? A user describes an experiment (fuel, oxygen, pressure, gravity) and receives five cited answers: has it been done, what is missing, what to run next, what we expect, and a written brief. Behind this are 23 NASA PSI combustion investigations ranked by seven visible, adjustable features; a coverage map of gaps on oxygen and pressure; 39 oxygen-extinction points from the SoFIE-GEL experiment; and two exploratory models, each with a model card, held-out results and a domain check. Every number carries a provenance label (verified, estimated from figure, unreviewed) and a source from 16 papers and reports. The assistant only explains structured outputs and never produces numbers. Limiar says plainly what it cannot do: PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data, so Moon and Mars estimates are labeled extrapolations. Limiar is Portuguese for "threshold", the point where a flame spreads or goes out.
Our landing page is the gate to the Vercel Dashboard.
details:
Limiar

Research workspace for the NASA Space Apps Challenge — "Flame in Freefall"


WHAT LIMIAR IS


Limiar is a research workspace built for the "Flame in Freefall" challenge. It turns NASA's microgravity and partial-gravity combustion records into a decision tool: a user describes a fire-safety experiment, and Limiar shows what has already been measured, where the evidence ends, what to test next, and what exploratory models expect — with every number traceable to its source. It is designed for professors, students, researchers and aerospace engineers. A Neutral / Student / Professor / Engineer switch changes the depth of the explanations, never the data. "Limiar" is Portuguese for threshold: the point where evidence stops, and the point where a flame spreads or goes out.

THE PROBLEM

Results from low-gravity combustion experiments are public in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, but they are hard to find, harder to compare and harder to interpret. At the same time, lunar habitats are expected to run at about 30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less, where materials burn more easily — and PSI currently holds no partial-gravity combustion data. The question a designer needs answered is not "what do we know about fire in space?" but "what do we know about this fire, in this cabin?" Limiar is built to answer that question, and to say clearly when the honest answer is "not enough".

HOW IT WORKS: THE WORKSPACE

The workspace has eight numbered tabs, a node-based canvas (Node Workspace) and an assistant.

01 Experiment Planner

The user sets fuel, atmosphere and gravity. Five presets are provided:

Preset

O₂

Five cited answers follow.

(1) Prior art: the closest measured sources, ranked by how many axes match, with a "Why this rank" for each; a near match counts half, and a source that does not state an axis never counts as a match. For the Challenge preset, the closest measured source (TAK_PMMA, the Takahashi aircraft thin-PMMA film experiment) confirms 4 of 5 axes.

(2) Gaps: which axes no single source covers, and where PSI has nothing. For the same preset, the answer is "no single source covers all 3 axes together", with the closest sources at 2/3 axes.

(3) Next experiment: a rule-based proposal that says what to vary, hold and measure, on which platform, why, and with what uncertainty. For the Challenge preset, the proposal is an oxygen ladder at 0.17 g and 70.3 kPa — 24, 27, 30 and 33% O₂, on a parabolic-flight aircraft (18–28 s of partial gravity per parabola), bracketing 30% so the outcome can flip inside the ladder.

(4) Prediction: the exploratory models' expectation, with a domain check and the nearest real cases. For the Challenge preset, MARGIN-Spread returns "Flame spreads" at log-odds +11.16, flagged as an extrapolation because 30% O₂ is outside the trained range (15–21%).

(5) Brief: a written summary that the assistant composes from the four parts above and nothing else, or a fixed no-AI template over the same parts, so every sentence can be checked. The plan exports as JSON.

02 Investigations

23 NASA PSI investigations (microgravity and ground-based, covering ACME CFI-G, BASS-II, SAFFIRE-I/II/III, FLEX, FLEX-2, BASS, SAME, SAME-R, ACME/Flame Design, ACME BRE, ACME E-FIELD, ACME CLD Flame, SLICE, CFI, SPICE, ACME s-Flame, PSI-62, PSI-142, PSI-115, PSI-117 and PSI-60) are scored for a habitat target. Each score is a weighted mean of seven visible features. The user can change the weights, filter by environment (spacecraft, space station, Moon base, pressurized rover) and by pillar (prevention, detection, suppression, complementary), open a "Why this rank" breakdown for every row, and export the table as CSV. Each row states its fuel type, number of files and that its fields are unreviewed. The score is relative to Moon-base priorities, not a measure of quality, and keyword counts mean "mentioned in the PSI text", not "measured".

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Investigations tab" ]

03 Compare

Two to four investigations side by side, with differences highlighted and never averaged away ("Same question, different tests.").

04 Coverage and Gaps

Every measured source and dataset we hold is drawn as a box on an oxygen versus pressure map, with the user's experiment as a cross. A box is a range the source swept, not a guarantee that every point inside was tested. Recorded gaps carry a VERIFIED label:

  • (a) no partial-gravity combustion data in PSI (LUCI and FM2 are expected to add some);
  • (b) FLEX has 24 of 274 tests at 30% O₂ or more, but none at or below 10.2 psi (17 of them sit at 10.2–10.6 psi), and FLEX burned liquid droplets in microgravity, not solids in partial gravity.

A button turns any gap into a proposed experiment.

05 Evidence

39 oxygen-extinction points for 4 cm PMMA spheres at 1 atm in microgravity on the ISS (SoFIE-GEL, T'ien et al. 2025): 5 verified from Table 2 and 34 read from Figure 8, each labeled.

Points are classified by regime (quenching, in-between, stagnation blow-off, total blow-off) over flows from 0.359 to 77.239 cm/s.
A quadratic trend in log₁₀(flow) is fitted in the browser with a 90% prediction band (residual sd 0.92% O₂, leave-one-out error 0.97% O₂, minimum ≈14.1% O₂ at 37.7 cm/s).

Clicking a point shows its source, condition and confidence. The data exports as CSV. The page states that the fit is unreliable below about 0.4 cm/s and valid only for PMMA spheres at 1 atm in microgravity.

06 Estimator (MARGIN-Spread)

For an already-burning thin sample in partial gravity, the user moves gravity, oxygen, pressure, thickness and material and sees an estimated outcome (spreads or extinguishes) as an uncalibrated log-odds score, never a probability. A domain check marks each input INSIDE or OUTSIDE its trained span:

Input

Trained span

Gravity

0.0833–0.375 g

Oxygen

15–21%

Pressure

56.5–101.3 kPa

Thickness

0.05–0.125 mm

Material

ACRYPLEN, Filter paper

The nearest real cases appear beside the estimate. Gravity is limited to 0.05–0.6 g because 0 g and 1 g behave non-monotonically: they appear as measured reference points and are never interpolated.

07 Model Cards

For each model: the question it answers, the method, the data, the trained domain, the held-out results, the known failures, what it does not claim, and how to reproduce it (commands and a SHA-256 hash of the weights).

08 Sources and Method

16 papers, reports and slide sets with citation, license and provenance, and a BibTeX export. Three provenance labels, shown by shape as well as color, are never mixed: verified, estimated from figure and unreviewed.

Node Workspace

A node-based canvas for building a recipe: Scenario, MARGIN-Spread, Domain check, Nearest evidence and Evidence chart nodes connected by typed wires. A wire inherits the weakest provenance among its inputs, so an estimate can never look more certain than the data behind it. A provenance key and an inspector show values and sources for any selected node or wire. One recipe ships with the app ("Moon estimate"), which deliberately opens outside the model's domain to show what an extrapolation looks like.

Ask Limiar

A conversational assistant called Lhai.
It explains the structured outputs above, cites their node IDs, and never produces numbers of its own.

DATA AND PROVENANCE

NASA PSI supplies 23 combustion investigations (metadata and text for all; experimental tables for most). Peer-reviewed and technical literature supplies the measured evidence for the models:

  • Takahashi et al. 2026 — 38 partial-gravity cases from 18 flights; 24 spread, 14 extinguished; outcomes estimated from Fig. 7 and joined to the Table S1 conditions.
  • T'ien et al. 2025 — 39 extinction points.

The knowledge graph on the Sources tab links 101 nodes and 104 edges: 16 papers, 15 measured evidence items, 23 PSI investigations, 18 quoted numeric limits and 13 summaries.

No row on the site is synthetic.

THE TWO MODELS

MARGIN-Spread is a standardized logistic regression on the 38 Takahashi cases (6 features: gravity, oxygen, pressure, thickness, and a material one-hot). Held-out checks:

Check

Correct

Leave-1/6 g out

12 / 17

Leave-3/8 g out

9 / 12

Fixed-seed split, chosen post-hoc (32 train / 6 held out)

5 / 6

Full fit in-sample

34 / 38 (not a validation)

A stricter split that also holds out repeated conditions lowers balanced accuracy from 0.85 to 0.82. We also tested physics-based features, a Gaussian-process classifier, an unpenalized intercept and Firth regression; none improved the result, and we report that in the model card instead of hiding it.

MARGIN-Limit is a quadratic trend of extinction oxygen against log₁₀(flow) fitted to the SoFIE-GEL points with a 90% prediction band. Both are exploratory, retrospective and explicit about what they do not claim.

The live model weights are shipped as JSON and scored in the browser; the SHA-256 hash of the weights is: 281F5C6022FADC34A43D36F802E80950542DFB36770D3F21C897AC6C6FB51058

THE USE OF AI

The assistant writes only from the planner's four structured parts, cites node IDs and creates no numbers, so a reader can check any sentence against its source. A no-AI summary is always available. AI tools were also used by the team during development (code, data extraction, text drafting); the central idea is the team's. See the SI disclosure.

TECHNOLOGY

Data processing and model export (Python 3.12)

Python 3.12 for data processing and model export:

  • pymupdf, numpy, opencv, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib
  • anonymous boto3 access to the public NASA PSI bucket

Database

SQLite for the PSI database.

Knowledge graph

Node.js scripts to build the knowledge graph.

Web application

A React 19 + Vite 8 web application:

  • @xyflow/react 12 (React Flow) for the Node Workspace
  • zustand 5 for state
  • In-browser fitting for the live curve and the estimator (no backend for the models — only the assistant uses a serverless function)

Website and visual

Framer and Vercel

Assistant

The assistant uses Google Gemini 2.5 Flash through Vercel serverless functions (/api/chat and /api/parse), with the API key held only on the server.

Reproducibility

Models are reproducible with:

python src/export_takahashi_live_model.py
python src/sync_web_data.py

The weights carry a SHA-256 hash.

WHAT WE CHOSE NOT TO DO

  • Limiar does not predict fire risk, ignition, heat release, flame size or habitat safety.
  • Its estimates are not calibrated probabilities.
  • It does not count a source as matching an axis the source never states.
  • It does not mix verified, figure-estimated and unreviewed data.
  • The model validation is retrospective on figure-derived labels and is not independent.
  • Moon and Mars are reached by analogy and extrapolation, always shown with a domain check.
  • Earth applications of this research (fine-water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection, firefighter gear) are context only; there is no model for them.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

For a researcher or engineer, Limiar shortens the path from "I want to test this condition" to "here is what exists, what is missing and what to run next".

For a student, it makes the structure of the evidence visible.

For the field, it records the gaps in a machine-readable, sourced form (for example, the absence of partial-gravity data in PSI and the absence of FLEX tests at 30% O₂ and 10.2 psi or below), so that future data from LUCI and FM2 can be placed directly on the same map.

It also aligns with SDG 9 (test planning), SDG 17 (citable, reusable data and methods) and SDG 3 (crew safety as motivation, without claiming a clinical result).

CREATIVITY

The project's core idea is to treat uncertainty as the product. The interface is organized around the threshold of its name: the point where evidence stops. Provenance labels are carried by shape as well as color, a wire in the Node Workspace inherits the weakest provenance of its inputs, every model ships with a card that lists its known failures, and the assistant is restricted to explaining structured outputs. We report negative results (methods that did not improve the model) alongside the positive ones.

The planner's five answers are computed by visible rules, not typed in by hand — the interface itself says so:

"Everything on the right is computed from your inputs by visible rules; nothing is typed in by hand."

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Scientific honesty over impressiveness.
  • The small and retrospective nature of the data (38 Takahashi cases, 39 SoFIE-GEL points).
  • Licensing: T'ien et al. 2025 is CC BY-NC-ND (numbers are cited, the figure is not redistributed); Takahashi et al. 2026 is CC BY.
  • Accessibility: color is never the only carrier of meaning; shape carries provenance too.
  • Reproducibility: SHA-256 hash and reproduction commands.
  • Different audiences, from students to engineers (the Neutral / Student / Professor / Engineer switch).

TRY IT IN 60 SECONDS

  1. Open the Planner and choose the preset "Challenge lunar-habitat bound" (30% O₂, 70.3 kPa, 0.165 g).
    • the closest measured source matches 4 of 5 axes;
    • no single source covers all 3 axes;
    • PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data;
    • a parabolic-flight oxygen ladder (24, 27, 30, 33% O₂) is proposed;
    • the model flags the 30% O₂ input as outside its trained range (log-odds +11.16, labeled extrapolation).
  2. Open Coverage and Gaps to see the cross fall outside every box.
  3. Open Sources to see every number's provenance.

ACCESS

You may access the project's dashboard codebase on:
https://github.com/N-The-K-3403/limiar-spaceapps

Commit history shows that the project started and stopped development on November 14-15 under UTC-3, following the spirit of the hackathon.

TEAM

We are three brazillians, working together interstate:


Elias Aguiar de Moraes, Iker Torres Serpa, Maria Eduarda Machado Mendes.

“Every time a scientific paper presents a bit of data, it's accompanied by an error bar – a quiet but insistent reminder that no knowledge is complete or perfect.
It's a calibration of how much we trust what we think we know. If the error bars are small, the accuracy of our empirical knowledge is high; if the error bars are large, then so is the uncertainty in our knowledge.”

― Carl Sagan.
